Someone asked why wouldn't Asia just take more West African (WAF) crudes and let the Saudi grades get absorbed by Europe if the big rerouting via Suez Canal happens?

It all boils down to quality. Asia can take some WAF as displacement for the Middle East crudes, but because of the high nitrogen and high TAN of the WAF grades, the refinery hits a limit fast.

That's why we didn't see WAF getting wolfed up by Korea or Japan throughout the crisis. If China is not there to buy WAF, it becomes distressed.

For those not familiar with the logistics surrounding the alternative routes for Saudi crude if the Bab el-Mandeb Strait becomes shut <editted>:  

1⃣ You normally load VLCCs (Very Large Crude Carriers) which take 2 mb of crude from Yanbu currently and Ras Tanura when Strait of Hormuz is open.   

2⃣ These VLCCs are typically the most cost economic way to freight Middle Eastern crude into Asia.  

3⃣ If the VLCC cannot transit Bab el-Mandeb strait, then it has to go north up the Red Sea and go to Ain Sukhna port, discharge part of the 2 mb cargo into the Sumed pipeline and transit via the Suez Canal at a lighter draft, to then reload the balance cargo from Sidi Kerir. Then this VLCC goes a biggggggg round from the Mediterranean Sea, make a bigggggg detour round the Cape of Good Hope to go into Asia. This extra step takes about 30 days and a lot more handling cost. <Use Google Maps to visualize what I just said>

4⃣Another way is to load the crude at Yanbu with Suezmaxes which can take 1 mb of cargo only. Use this Suezmax to transit via the Suez Canal and do that whole rerouting using the Med Sea and Cape of Good Hope. Chartering Suezmax to load 2 mb of cargo generally economically unfavourable compared to the VLCC option, but the new VLCC option is really quite bad as well.  

5⃣If your cargo HAS loaded already on a VLCC, you would need to use the Sumed pipeline way, or split the cargo into 2 Suezmax to utilize the Suez Canal way.  

All the above is $$$$$ and extra time (not to mention vessel losses also).  

#oott

Asking for help from the shipping community: 

Is the Suez Canal truly bidirectional? I.e. can we see VLCCs on ballast coming from Med into the Red Sea to load Yanbu cargoes if the Bab el Mandeb Strait is closed? #oott

Hi folks, sorry I made an error with my point 3. The VLCC that unloads some cargo to the SUMED pipeline can then travel through the Suez Canal at a lighter draft, and reload the discharged oil at Sidi Kerir on the Med side. So you don't need to charter a whole new VLCC for the second leg of the voyage.

Thanks for all who pointed out the mistake.

Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, said on Sunday that the Strait of Hormuz's status remains unchanged, as Iranian and Omani officials continued talks to manage the safe transit of ships through the waterway that passes between both countries.

Baghaei said the talks had made progress. They took place after Tehran asserted 

that its interim deal with the U.S. allows it to manage shipping in the strait for now, and objected to U.S. efforts to support a route through the strait that passes close to Oman instead. The strait was considered an international waterway before the war. https://t.co/fMr9eyMpUG
